t: Eleven forty-one at night. You stand at a stranger's door, out of breath.
Above you, a twenty-nine is blinking. Not counted yet. Above the one who opened the door, too.
What's up? You ran across the whole district.
In nineteen minutes both counters turn to zero. To stop that, you need eleven.
Let me in. We have eleven minutes for two.
What if a counter of days hung over you, and one missed day burned it?
Let's rewind twenty-nine days.
Day one. You stand at a door with a sign that says Boxing, pretending for the third time that you're just passing by.
You have exactly one reason: you're tired of flinching when someone raises a hand fast.
You walk in. And a one lights up over your head.
What's that?
You look around. Numbers hang over everyone who trains here.
The old man with the jump rope: fourteen hundred. The girl at the bag: two hundred twelve.
Big Vovan: forty-one. He's proud of it and stands so everyone can see.
New guy? Wraps first. The hand is made of small bones.
Wraps hold the small bones of your hand. So they don't break on your very first bag.
Group enrollment in thirty-three days. Three are for sickness.
I take only those with thirty over their heads.
Nobody explains the counter rules. Everyone knows only the main one.
Miss a day, and at midnight it burns to zero. And everyone sees it.
Next to you, a guy in red is tangled in his wraps. He has a one, too.
Tyoma. First day, too. Can you help? I got tangled.
Sanya. Hold your finger here.
Jump rope. Ten minutes. That's boxing, too.
At exactly seven thirty p.m., Tyoma grabs his bag and runs. Without saying goodbye.
Day three. Everything hurts. Even muscles you didn't know you had.
Muscles hurt most one to three days after a workout. You're right at the peak.
Evening. No strength for the gym. You decide stretching on a mat counts as training.
You google what the counter counts. The internet offers you a pedometer.
A small heart appears next to the tag for the first time. Gray. Eighty beats a minute.
Eleven forty-five. The tag blinks red.
What?! But I stretched! Twenty minutes!
The counter doesn't need a checkmark. It needs work. The heart has to pound.
Kitchen. Jump rope. Three rounds of three minutes, like at the gym. A timer on your phone.
The heart turns red: one-twenty, one-forty, one-fifty.
Mom appears in the doorway. Looks at you. Looks at the chandelier. Leaves without a word.
Eleven fifty-six. Green.
Rule one. Effort counts. Not a checkmark, not noise, but how your heart beats.
For the next week you and Tyoma test the counter like scientists. Your lab is the yard behind the garages.
Experiment one. How much does it take to count?
One round, and at night the tag blinks. Two rounds, it still blinks.
Writing it down: fewer than three doesn't count. Moving science forward.
Split the Nobel.
Every time, you finish what's missing before midnight. Checking is scary.
Three rounds of three minutes with a minute of rest, and it glows green. That's how adult amateurs fight.
Experiment two. No bag, no pads.
Shadowboxing in the yard. Heart one-fifty. Counted. The place doesn't matter.
Experiment three happens by accident. In the middle of round two, Tyoma's mom calls.
Yes, Mom. Yes. He ate.
Thirty seconds of talking. The heart fades. And that round burns.
You stopped, so start the round over. The counter sees every pause.
Experiment four is Tyoma's idea.
Let's just run. Running is easier.
Ten minutes of steady running. The heart is yellow, one twenty-five. Not counted. The pulse doesn't reach.
So running is useless?
For the counter, yes. For your legs, no.
Rule two. Three rounds. No stopping. The place doesn't matter. Steady running doesn't count.
And again seven thirty, and Tyoma runs off. Every day, at the same time.
Where do you think he goes? We'll come back to it.
Elbow! Chin! Breathe!
Your arms are the same as a week ago. But the punches are faster and more accurate.
In the first weeks, strength grows mostly because the brain learns to switch the muscles on. The muscles catch up later.
Day twelve. Smack, and the coach nods for the first time.
Day fifteen. In the morning the thermometer shows thirty-eight point two.
You drag yourself to the gym anyway. In a scarf, with a red nose and a blinking fifteen over your head.
With a fever, go home. Right now.
But the counter?! It'll burn!
If it burns, you start over. You've got one head.
Midnight. The counter doesn't burn. It turns gray. A small word on top: pause.
Three days of gray pause. Tyoma's too: you caught a cold together, in the yard. You recover, and it's fifteen again.
For all three days you check the gray tag every half hour. Like a thermometer.
And Vovan decided he'd found a loophole.
He texts the coach: sick. And goes to the movies.
Midnight. His forty-one doesn't turn gray. It burns. To zero.
By morning the photo of his zero is already in the gym's group chat.
Rule three. Illness freezes the counter. Lying burns it. And the counter knows the difference.
Day eighteen. Seven thirty. Tyoma runs off again. This time you follow.
Tyoma isn't going for a walk. He's running home. At the entrance his mom waits in scrubs.
She's leaving for a night shift at the hospital. And Tyoma stays with his little brother. Until morning.
What are you doing here? Were you following me?
Why didn't you say?
What's there to say? It's not laziness. It just happened.
I thought you were just slacking.
Everyone thinks so. Let them.
Mom is alone. Hospital at night, sleeping in the day. Around eight the door closes behind Tyoma until morning.
Gym until nine. And I have to run at seven thirty.
Then let's do it here. Under the window. I'll hold the pads.
Three rounds under the window. The brother watches from above and counts the punches out loud.
At twenty-nine the brother loses count and starts over. Nobody minds.
In the middle of round two Tyoma's shoelace comes undone. The knot pulls tight. Tyoma fights with it for almost a minute.
And all that time you keep moving with the pads, not standing for a second. And somehow Tyoma's heart doesn't fade.
Midnight. You're home, looking at your tag. Green. Though today you never threw a punch yourself.
Strange. They counted both. Even Tyoma with the shoelace.
Day twenty-two. Two tests in a row. You come home and sit down for a minute.
You open your eyes. Eleven forty-one.
No, no, no, no!
The apartment sleeps. You dash onto the stairs. Three rounds of shadowboxing between floors.
You count the seconds in a whisper, so you don't wake the neighbors. The heart pounds louder than you.
Eleven fifty-three. Done. Green.
The next day you tell it at the gym. The old man with the jump rope silently draws in the air with a finger: zero zero, zero two.
Once he finished two minutes after midnight. And everything burned. Since then, fourteen hundred.
Rule four. Don't start before midnight. Finish.
Day twenty-nine. Tomorrow is thirty, and with it the tournament group. Today is your sister's concert.
Mom's on shift. There's no dad. You're the one going to the concert. You promised a month ago.
Your sister sings off key and loud. You clap louder than anyone.
The concert runs seven to nine. The gym closes at nine. You choose the concert.
Then you sit with your sister until Mom is back. Like Tyoma. Only for you it's one evening.
Eleven o'clock. Mom's home. You wrap your hands. Eleven minutes, and the counter is saved.
Eleven oh two. You call Tyoma to do the rounds at the same time, like last week.
My brother has thirty-eight and a half.
Mom said: a cool towel every two minutes.
I started twice. Every two minutes, stop.
That's it, Sanya. I'm out.
Illness freezes the counter. But it's the brother who's sick, not Tyoma. His twenty-eight days will burn.
Eleven oh five. Two paths.
First: your own rounds at home, until eleven sixteen. Your counter is saved.
Then a run to Tyoma. Thirty-six minutes. You're at his door at eleven fifty-two.
Tyoma starts at fifty-five and finishes at six past midnight. After midnight. Zero.
Second path: run right now. But your own rounds aren't done yet.
Finish at home, and that's it?
You tear off the wraps. And run out.
The buses don't run anymore. Five kilometers of steady running. You can't go faster.
Eleven twenty-three. Halfway. Your legs are like cotton, but you keep a steady pace.
Heart: one-thirty. Yellow. Running doesn't count, you tested it yourself in the yard.
Eleven thirty. How do you fit two elevens into eleven minutes?
The shoelace!
Eleven forty-one. A stranger's door. You can't catch your breath. Now you know why you ran.
Let me in. We'll do them together.
You could've done it all at home.
I could. Let me in, it's time.
Eleven forty-four. A basin by the bed. A stack of towels. Pads wrapped so they don't slap. The brother sleeps two steps away.
One rule against you: stop, and the round burns. But in a pair, the round goes on while at least one of you works.
Tap, don't hit. Quietly. When I change the towel, you don't stop.
And when I change it?
Then I work. Let's go.
Round one. Light taps, almost no sound. But footwork, slips, tempo. Both hearts turn red.
Eleven forty-six. You step to the bed. Fifteen seconds. Tyoma punches the air and doesn't stop.
Eleven forty-seven. Rest. At eleven forty-seven thirty, a fresh towel while you rest.
Round two. Eleven fifty. Tyoma goes to his brother. And you work with empty pads: duck, step, duck.
Eleven fifty-one. Rest. At fifty-one thirty, a towel again. Round three. The last one.
Eleven fifty-four. You're at the bed again. The brother opens his eyes and looks at you.
Eleven fifty-five. The timer hits zero. You slide down the wall.
The brother stands in the doorway. With a towel on his forehead.
When you get better. I promise.
Midnight. The twenty-nine over both of you stops blinking.
The next day, thirty. The coach writes two names on the board.
Both. Into the group.
Day forty-one. You're wiped out. Nine p.m., you sit on the bed, and that's it.
Midnight. Forty days in a row turn into zero.
By morning the photo of your zero is already in the group chat. You lie there staring at the ceiling.
On the fridge hangs your sister's card: "Forty days for Sanya!" She drew it yesterday.
Forty days. To zero. Why even get up?
Forty days. And that's all.
Your legs carry you to the gym. By themselves. You don't remember lacing up.
At the gym, Vovan. The one whose forty-one burned at the movies.
Above him, twenty-nine. He wraps his hands without looking. Like brushing teeth.
You burned. Why did you come?
Vovan shrugs and points at his sneakers. As if to say, they did it themselves.
He didn't start over out of grief. He just kept coming.
Scientists looked for the moment when you do it on autopilot.
For a typical person, sixty-six. One missed day changed almost nothing.
That's a study from University College London. The spread is from eighteen to two hundred fifty-four days.
A habit didn't form in people who missed often. And one missed day barely touched it.
And this is about habit. Showing up without talking yourself into it. How you punch is a different score.
The tag over you blinks. And changes. Now it shows not days in a row, but habit.
Zero was never the end. The counter was just counting the wrong thing.
Day sixty-six. Your bar is almost full. Tyoma's is shorter. Everyone has their own time.
Looks like mine is all two hundred fifty-four.
Then I'll come with you for all two hundred fifty-four.
The coach no longer looks at the tags. He looks at where your elbows are.
Elbow!
Evening. Tyoma's mom is on shift again. In the yard under the window, three shadows.
Over the smallest one, a one lights up.
And you? What did you quit after your first miss? Be honest.
In a month, a tournament. And that same evening, Tyoma's mom has a night shift again.
